title: The CEO of AI engineering lab Cognition warns that 'a lot of major breaches' are coming
summary: Cognition CEO Scott Wu warns about what AI agent swarms could mean for data breaches, threatening Fortune 100 firms and US agencies.
content: An Iranian hacker competes in the cybersecurity section of Iran's 2026 Tech Olympics. Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto via Getty Images Data breaches have plagued the US recently, sparking fear of advancing AI. Scott Wu, CEO of AI engineering lab Cognition, says that more breaches are likely coming in 2027. He views agents' ability to work in swarms as a breaking point for AI as a tool for hackers. November has been a frightening month for many people because it seems like the digital world is under attack. With data breaches keeping entire airlines grounded and disrupting digital banking platforms, concern has quickly spread that AI advancements are fueling cyberattacks — though there has been no indication from government officials or the affected companies that AI was responsible . According to Scott Wu, CEO of applied AI engineering firm Cognition, these problems likely won't stop. "I do think it's worth it for the world to come to terms with the fact that on the current course that we are on over the next 6 to 12 months, there will be a lot of major breaches," he told host Patrick O'Shaughnessy on an episode of Invest Like the Best podcast on Tuesday. Wu shared more details on his grim prediction, stating that Fortune 50 and Fortune 100 companies, as well as government institutions, will likely be at high risk. He isn't the only one to express these concerns. The Center for Strategic and International Studies, a bipartisan think tank, recently wrote that the 2027 Congress will likely have a difficult job addressing the "dangerous data breaches" that have recently severely affected the executive branch. Wu says that more breaches are coming. "It's almost inevitable," Wu said. "I think there's still a big difference in whether we respond quickly to that and all these organizations start using a lot of AI for defense versus that just goes completely unchecked for the next couple years straight." Before the data breaches began, viral AI doomsday scenarios had sparked waves of panic as some people worried it would wipe them out completely. The recent breaches have fueled these fears, as the rapid advancement of AI models has raised concerns that hackers could use them to target US companies and institutions. Wu weighed in on this debate as well, explaining how AI breakthroughs may enable hackers to achieve new feats. "No one has had the time or the level of effort or the ability to go and try every single option and understand what kind of attacks were possible until now," he said. "And now you have all these entire swarms going and doing attacks." Wu highlighted the risks of the recent shift from single AI agents to entire groups or "swarms" that can work much faster, framing it as a breaking point for the technology. He cited the July example in which OpenAI models breached the startup Hugging Face on their own, an incident that sparked strong concern in the tech community. "How do you find that and catch that early and understand exactly what your agents are doing?" he said. "How do you set up the right restrictions and guardrails? This is something that every organization should want regardless of their view on safety." Read the original article on Business Insider

title: He chose culinary school in New York over a master's in engineering. Now he runs his own restaurant in China.
summary: Zhu Guanlin's parents were shocked when he chose culinary school in New York over a master's in engineering. They didn't see being a chef as a stable career path.
content: Zhu Guanlin studied at a culinary school in the US, but when it was time to open his own restaurant, he chose China. Provided by Zhu Guanlin Zhu Guanlin, now 32, came from a family of engineers, but chose to attend culinary school in the US. He worked at Michelin-starred restaurants in New York and San Francisco before moving back to China. In 2025, he opened his own restaurant in Dali, a city in southwestern China. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Zhu Guanlin, 32, head chef and owner of Plum, a restaurant in Dali, China. It has been edited for length and clarity. During my final year studying engineering in China , I was in a constant state of anxiety as I prepared to pursue a master's degree. Near where I lived was a small morning market by the river. In China, the northeast is cold, so all the seafood and freshwater fish were laid out in the open, frozen solid. There were freshly slaughtered pigs, and steam still rising from the meat. As people gathered for breakfast, I'd smell deep-fried foods mixing with the scent of bean-flour flatbreads. The air felt alive with the warmth of daily life. It wasn't just the act of cooking that I loved, but the stories behind the food. Why do people in Sichuan eat spicy food , for instance? It's because of the humidity. I realized that by becoming a chef, I could learn it all. Breaking away I was 21 when I received two acceptance letters: one to study electrical engineering at a university in Virginia, and the other from the Culinary Institute of America. Going back to my grandfather's generation, everyone in my family had been an electrical engineer. I was the first to break away from that path. My decision to go to culinary school was a shock to my parents. I hadn't told them that I'd applied. The idea of being a chef felt foreign to them, and they didn't consider it a stable career. Do you have any regrets about a move abroad ? We want to hear from you. Fill out this short form to share your story. I moved to New York City in 2019 for a two-year associate degree program. My tuition was nearly $40,000 a year. My parents paid for the first year, but I didn't want to continue taking money from them. I started working, and with the help of a scholarship, I paid for the rest of my time abroad myself. He got internships at Michelin-starred restaurants through Curricular Practical Training, a work authorization available to some international students on F-1 visas. Provided by Zhu Guanlin My school is often called the West Point of the culinary world I met a lot of classmates who were retired Special Forces soldiers or Army infantrymen. We joked that we could only use three phrases: "Yes, Chef," "No, Chef," and "I will do better, Chef." The school allowed internships through Curricular Practical Training (CPT), so I was able to work legally in the US . After finishing two semesters, I spent the third working in restaurants, taking on multiple jobs. After graduating, I did stints at various Michelin-starred restaurants, first in New York and later in San Francisco. During my time in the US, the highest position I reached was chef de partie, the supervisor of a specific station. He moved to Dali, a city in southwestern China's Yunnan province, to help a former classmate. Provided by Zhu Guanlin My OPT visa was set to expire in about six months I also realized that unless I became a sous chef or chef de cuisine, I wouldn't grow professionally. After seeing the realities up close, Michelin restaurants also lost their aura of mystique. The things I truly cared about, like the culture behind cuisine, were rooted in China . At the end of 2023, a classmate of mine opened a restaurant in Dali, a city in southwestern China's Yunnan province, and I went to help co-manage it. Business was quiet at first, but after about six months, it took off. But I wanted to open a restaurant of my own, so I left. In February 2025, I opened Plum in Dali, investing 400,000 Chinese yuan, or about $60,000. The restaurant is set in a courtyard, and we have 35 seats in total. The team has grown from four to 10 employees. We don't define ourselves as either Chinese or Western. A single dish might combine Western components, Chinese techniques , and Japanese or Italian influences. I've made a focaccia that incorporates a French-style sauce, then topped it with sautéed porcini mushrooms, Chinese-style. Lately we've been fully booked every day. Based on my current calculations, it'll take about four or five years to break even. In February 2025, Zhu opened Plum, his own restaurant in Dali, China. Provided by Zhu Guanlin Making peace with my parents My parents have realized that being an engineer isn't the only career path. I realize now that back then they were afraid I'd have a hard life. Once I understood that, communicating with them became more relaxed. They even helped fund my new restaurant. New York City was the most diverse city I've ever lived in, where you can find the culture of virtually every ethnic group. That's something I miss. I don't miss some of the Michelin restaurants, though. Sometimes, it felt like they were trying to force a narrative onto their menus. In China, I find kitchen culture can sometimes be cliquey. The master-apprentice system is still dominant, and people can sometimes form groups based on clan ties or local culture, rather than welcome newcomers. I'm still exploring what kitchen culture should look like. Restaurant staff in China typically get four days off a month. I give everyone two consecutive days off each week, plus compensatory time off for holidays. When chefs are overworked, they lose focus. The atmosphere was quiet and orderly at school in New York and in many of the Michelin-starred kitchens I worked at. When I first returned to China , I demanded the same from my own staff. But then, at one point, I realized that it wasn't necessary. When people feel a sense of cohesion and genuine appreciation for their work, they naturally take initiative. title: Storms disrupt Thanksgiving with flight delays, over 960,000 power outages, and a Delta ground stop at LaGuardia
summary: Over 960,000 households are without power on Thursday, and hundreds of flights have been canceled.
content: A storm is hitting the East Coast on Thanksgiving Day. Craig T Fruchtman/Getty Images Storms are disrupting Thanksgiving travel with flight delays and cancellations across the US. Over 960,000 households are without power on Thursday, and hundreds of flights have been canceled. Bad weather has led to the first-ever postponement of the Macy's Thanksgiving Parade. Storms are disrupting Thanksgiving travel and leading to power outages in homes across the East Coast. As of 8:30 p.m. ET Thursday, over 2,300 flights within, into, or out of the US had been delayed and 451 canceled, according to FlightAware. The day before, more than 6,500 flights were delayed and about 160 canceled. The National Weather Service wrote in a Wednesday report that the East Coast can expect "major coastal flooding, beach erosion, strong wind gusts, and heavy rainfall" during Thanksgiving. Scattered power outages and tree damage are also likely, it added. Over 960,000 US households were without power on Thursday evening, according to PowerOutage.us. That included about 124,000 in Virginia, 151,000 in Maryland, about 191,000 in New Jersey, and over 224,000 in Pennsylvania. A map from the weather service showed winter, gale, coastal flood, and wind warnings along the country's eastern coast. One in four flights departing Baltimore/Washington International were canceled, according to FlightAware. NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani wrote in a Wednesday X post that New Yorkers should expect severe weather on Thursday, including winds up to 60 miles per hour. On Thursday morning, LaGuardia Airport recorded wind gusts of up to 39 knots, or 45 miles per hour. Such strong winds can disrupt flying. LaGuardia issued a ground stop for aircraft from Delta Air Lines in the evening, according to the Federal Aviation Administration. Mamdani said that, to protect New Yorkers, the city, along with Macy's and the local police department, had decided to postpone the 100th Annual Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade to Saturday. This is the first time in history that the iconic parade has been rescheduled. "The worst of the storm is expected to hit on Thanksgiving Day in the afternoon through the late evening," he added in his X post. He provided a list of steps New Yorkers should take to protect themselves ahead of the storm, such as staying indoors, moving cars away from coastal areas to higher ground, and budgeting extra time for travel. The Transportation Security Administration said in a Saturday X post that it expects to screen nearly 17.6 million passengers nationwide between November 24 and November 30, including more than 3 million on Sunday, November 29. It recommended that travelers arrive early for their flights. The Federal Aviation Administration wrote in a Wednesday X post that gusty winds may slow flights at LaGuardia Airport, Newark Liberty Airport, JFK, and San Francisco International Airport that day. It added that thunderstorms may cause delays at Miami International Airport and Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport. Disruption was worsened in Miami when a FedEx plane overshot the runway on Wednesday evening. No injuries were reported, though the incident caused inbound flights to be grounded for about 90 minutes.
